title: Norwegian Wood
author: Haruki Murakami
review: Murakami at his most grounded and heartbreaking. This isn't the surreal Murakami of wind-up birds and underground kingdoms — this is a quiet, devastating story about loss, desire, and the people who shape us in our twenties. Every member who's read it has underlined a different sentence as their favorite. That says everything.
synopsis: Toru Watanabe, navigating university life in 1960s Tokyo, is caught between two very different women — the beautiful, emotionally fragile Naoko, and the outgoing, vivacious Midori. A meditation on nostalgia, sexuality, and the persistence of memory.

title: The God of Small Things
author: Arundhati Roy
review: Roy's prose is so lush it's almost edible. This novel taught our members that language can be broken and rebuilt, that grammar is a suggestion, and that the most political stories are often the most personal. Read it slowly. Then read it again.
synopsis: In the town of Ayemenem in Kerala, fraternal twins Estha and Rahel navigate a world shaped by the Love Laws — the laws that lay down who should be loved, and how, and how much.

title: Kafka on the Shore
author: Haruki Murakami
review: If Norwegian Wood is Murakami's realist masterpiece, this is his surrealist one. Talking cats, fish falling from the sky, a library that exists outside of time — and somehow it all makes emotional sense. This is the book that convinced half our club to start writing magical realism.
synopsis: Fifteen-year-old Kafka Tamura runs away from home to escape an oedipal prophecy. Meanwhile, an old man named Nakata, who can talk to cats, embarks on his own journey. Their paths converge in ways that defy logic but not feeling.

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
review: The quietest devastating book we've ever read. Stevens the butler is so committed to not feeling that every suppressed emotion hits the reader like a freight train. Ishiguro proves that what a character doesn't say is more powerful than any monologue.
synopsis: An aging English butler takes a road trip through the countryside, reflecting on his decades of service, his relationship with a former housekeeper, and whether he has wasted his life in the pursuit of professional dignity.

title: Beloved
author: Toni Morrison
review: Morrison writes like the English language was invented specifically for her to use. 'Beloved' is a ghost story, a love story, a horror story, and a history lesson all at once. It's not easy reading. It shouldn't be. Some truths require effort to receive.
synopsis: Set after the American Civil War, Sethe, a former enslaved woman, is haunted — literally — by the ghost of her dead daughter. When a mysterious young woman named Beloved appears, Sethe's past begins to consume her present.

title: The Vegetarian
author: Han Kang
review: A woman stops eating meat. That's it. That's the premise. And somehow Han Kang turns this into the most unsettling, beautiful, violent meditation on bodily autonomy, desire, and resistance we've encountered. Three novellas, three perspectives, one slow-motion revolution.
synopsis: After a series of disturbing dreams, Yeong-hye decides to stop eating meat, setting off a chain of increasingly extreme reactions from her husband, her brother-in-law, and her sister.

title: If on a winter's night a traveler
author: Italo Calvino
review: A novel about reading novels. Calvino wrote the ultimate love letter to the act of reading, and it's also the most playful, inventive piece of metafiction ever constructed. This book broke several of our members' understanding of what fiction can do. In the best way.
synopsis: You, the Reader, begin reading Italo Calvino's new novel. But the book is defective, and you're plunged into a series of interrupted beginnings of different novels, each in a different genre, while trying to find the complete version.

title: A Suitable Boy
author: Vikram Seth
review: At 1,349 pages, this is our most ambitious recommendation. Seth recreates post-independence India with such affection and detail that you forget you're reading fiction. It's a marriage plot, a political novel, a social comedy, and a love letter to a country finding its identity.
synopsis: Set in 1950s India, Mrs. Rupa Mehra wants to find a suitable boy for her younger daughter Lata. What follows is a sprawling saga of four families navigating love, politics, religion, and the making of modern India.

title: Convenience Store Woman
author: Sayaka Murata
review: Keiko Furukura is one of the most original characters in contemporary fiction — a woman who finds genuine peace and purpose in the rituals of her convenience store job, while the world insists she should want more. It's funny, strange, and quietly radical.
synopsis: Keiko has worked in a Tokyo convenience store for eighteen years, perfectly content with her routine. When a new coworker enters her life, she's forced to confront society's expectations about what a 'normal' life looks like.

title: The Shadow Lines
author: Amitav Ghosh
review: Ghosh draws lines — between Calcutta and London, between memory and history, between the borders we draw on maps and the ones we draw in our minds. This slim novel packs the intellectual weight of a book three times its size. Essential reading for anyone trying to write about place.
synopsis: An unnamed narrator in Calcutta traces the connections between his family and an English family across decades, exploring how borders — national, personal, temporal — shape identity and memory.

title: Piranesi
author: Susanna Clarke
review: A labyrinth of infinite halls filled with statues and ocean tides. Clarke creates a world so vivid and strange that returning to reality after finishing this book feels like the real disorientation. If you love worldbuilding, this is a masterclass in less-is-more.
synopsis: Piranesi lives in a vast, beautiful House filled with thousands of halls, an ocean that covers the lower floors, and hundreds of statues. He believes himself to be one of only two living inhabitants. He is not entirely correct.

title: The White Tiger
author: Aravind Adiga
review: Balram Halwai's voice is so sharp it cuts. Adiga writes about class, ambition, and modern India with a wit that makes you laugh until you realize what you're laughing at. This book started a semester-long debate in our club about whether Balram is a hero or a villain. We never resolved it.
synopsis: In a series of letters to the Chinese Premier, Balram Halwai narrates his journey from a village in the 'Darkness' to becoming a successful entrepreneur in Bangalore, revealing the brutal truths behind India's economic rise.

title: Pachinko
author: Min Jin Lee
review: Four generations of a Korean family in Japan, and every single one of them breaks your heart in a different way. Lee writes about displacement, identity, and endurance with such restraint that the emotional impact sneaks up on you. Several members reported crying on public transport while reading this.
synopsis: Beginning in early 1900s Korea, a young woman's fateful decision to leave with a minister leads to a multi-generational saga of a Korean family's struggle for identity and belonging in Japan.

title: The Stranger
author: Albert Camus
review: The first line — 'Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday, I don't know' — is the most efficient character introduction in literature. Camus wrote the ultimate outsider novel in barely 100 pages. Read it in one sitting, then argue about it for a month. That's what we did.
synopsis: Meursault, an indifferent French Algerian, attends his mother's funeral, begins a casual relationship, and then commits a senseless murder — forcing a confrontation with society's demand for meaning and remorse.
